name: Awetí
confidence_why: Drude's 2011 acoustic study of Awetí stress, restated in Drude 2021 and in the orthography paper by Drude, Awete and Aweti 2019, puts stress on the last syllable of the stem with small listed exception classes, and Reiter 2011 states the same rule from her own corpus, adding only a hedged remark that the rare roots of three or more syllables tend to be penultimate, so nothing contradicts the record but everything that describes stress comes from the same two fieldworkers on one documentation project.

catalog_quote: As it is the case with many Tupian accent-languages, the stress in Awetí generally falls on the last syllable of the stem. [...] The general rule of stress in Awetí, that the last syllable of the stem carries the stress, is independent of the nasality or other segmental-structural features of the syllables, in particular of their vowel quality and their ‘weight’. This means that syllables with any vowel and with or without consonants in coda or onset position can carry stress. Stress is also independent of the word class. [...] The majority of suffixes, inflectional as well as derivational, do not change the stress position, which remains on the last syllable of the stem. Of the inflectional suffixes, only one mood suffix and one allomorph of a verbal aspect suffix attract the stress, and both are disyllabic. In the case of derivational suffixes, class-changing suffixes usually do not affect the stress. However, there are stems which are formed by derivational suffixes which don’t change the major class (noun, verb). These have the stress on the new last syllable (that is, on the derivational suffix).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (defined by Drude as the syllable's capacity to carry sentence-level/syntactic accentuation) falls on the last syllable of the stem (root). Weight, vowel quality and word class are irrelevant. The domain is the stem, not the word: the great majority of inflectional suffixes (aspect -ju/-(z)oko, mood -(t)u/-aw, negation -(y)ka, case suffixes) and class-changing derivational suffixes leave stress on the stem-final syllable, so a suffixed word is typically not stressed word-finally. Stress shifts to the suffix only with the purposive -°apan, the progressive allomorph -°eju, and derivational suffixes that do not change word class (-'at, -ka, -(t)ukat, -tej, -tut, nominal tense -(p)ut, -(z)ã'jap). Awetí is not tonal, and Drude 2021 hypothesises that accent is not phonologically contrastive (no minimal pairs found); the main acoustic correlate is pitch (rising contour on the stressed syllable), not intensity or duration.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No general secondary-stress rule is stated. Drude 2011 (40), p. 21, labels the nominal negation suffix -e'ym as carrying 'secondary stress' while main stress stays on the stem; stative verbs with the progressive allomorph -eju have two stressable syllables (stem-final and suffix /e/), the choice varying with speaker, style and rhythm, and in isolation both often get high pitch (33), p. 19. Intensity is nearly uniform across syllables and Drude explicitly hesitates to postulate trochaic feet (p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate stress in: some 30 verb stems ending in a lenis consonant + /e/ (o-tige, o-mỹje; the /e/ analysed as a thematic morph); a few verbs in final unstressed -ã (o-kangã); a large group of animate/plant nouns ending in -yt (pyringyt, takanyt, nukakyt) versus regular final-stressed kujãkyt, ekyt, tywyt; a few other nouns (takarĩ, momati, momatsaza) and the pronoun ozoza (groupal suffix -za unstressed); adverbs in fused unstressed -wo/-pe/-ti/-ko (kype, ypytako); most postpositions in -o (ewizako, pywo, 'apo); the postposition kyty with varying stress; second-position particles (weti, wene, wian, zanu, tene, wezanu). Final sentential particles are clitics without stress. Stress-attracting suffixes as listed in the rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word form (phonological word); stress is treated as a lexical property of the stem-final syllable realised through syntactic (sentence) accentuation, so citation forms in isolation show it. Drude notes (fn. 21) that some Tupí-Guaraní descriptions posit a domain larger than the word; his acoustic study (secs. 6-8) used single word forms and carrier sentences. Language as a whole (ca. 150 speakers in 2011, ca. 300 per Drude 2021); no dialect qualification.
new_statements.identity_note: Awetí (awet1244) as spoken in the Upper Xingu villages (Mato Grosso); Drude worked with the community 1998-2010 (DOBES project). No separate dialects are distinguished; Drude 2011 mentions only one lexical 'dialectal variant' (takarĩ ~ takanyt). Glottolog lists Drude 2011 under a working title ('Word accent and its manifestation in Awetí', pp. 189-218, as cited in Drude 2019); the published paper is 'Stress in Awetí and its acoustic correlates', Amerindia 35: 7-40, as Drude 2021's own bibliography confirms.

new_statements.quote: The stress in the mono- or disyllabic lexical roots falls on the only or on the last syllable. The only exceptions are disyllabic and also trisyllabic verb stems ending in /F/, where the word stress is on the penultimate syllable (e.g. (20) b., (21) a., (23) a.). [...] In general, there are few lexical roots in Awetí which consist of more than two syllables. The stress in such lexical roots, also in nominals, seems to be mostly on the penultimate syllable (e.g. (24) a.). In order to understand the complex rules for the respective stress patterns, more research is needed. new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's existing statement (Drude 2011: stress on the last syllable of the stem) and with its exception class (Drude 2011 sec. 4 (17): verbs ending in unstressed [lenis]+e have penultimate stress); adds prefix/suffix stress behaviour, secondary stress, particle classes and ideophone stress. The remark that longer roots are 'mostly' penultimate is a hedged observation that goes slightly beyond Drude's 'generally last syllable of the stem' but Reiter explicitly defers to further research.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last syllable of the lexical root (mono-/disyllabic roots: the only or last syllable); prefixes are always unstressed and most suffixes are unstressed, so stress is anchored to the root/stem rather than to the word edge. The '/F/' in the extracted text is a font-glyph artefact for /e/ (the cited examples are [a.ˈkɨ.tse] 'I cut', [ˈwɨ.ɾe] 'it finished'): verb stems ending in /e/ are stressed on the penult. Roots of three or more syllables 'seem to be mostly' penultimate-stressed; Reiter calls the rules complex and in need of more research. Ideophones follow the same final-stress norm in mono-/disyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 93: 'On word-level the stress pattern may change, and secondary stress is applied according to the ability of bound forms to attract stress or not. Prefixes are always unstressed. With regard to suffixes it could be observed that there are stressed and unstressed suffixes'; fn. 146: stressed suffixes are -eju, -tut and -(p)ut; unstressed (more frequent) include -an, -ap, -at, -aw, -e'ym, -ka/-yka, -tu, -ytu, -za, -zan, -zoko/-oko (citing Drude et al. forthcoming). Uninflected words divide into stressed and unstressed particles (p. 93).
new_statements.exceptions: Di- and trisyllabic verb stems ending in /e/ have penultimate stress; longer (3+ syllable) roots, nominals included, seem mostly penultimate; -(e)ju is stressed with active verbs but not with stative verbs; -(z)oko never changes the word's stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All four works describe the single Awetí community of the Upper Xingu (Awetí village, Mato Grosso); no dialects are distinguished. Reiter's data come from the DOBES Awetí corpus (recordings coded kal_.., tal_..); Kamaiurá Sabino is a native-speaker author writing 'Awetý'; Corrêa da Silva is comparative (Mawé/Awetí/Tupí-Guaraní) and cites Monserrat's 1970s Awetí data. Corrêa da Silva's only explicit accent rule is for Sateré-Mawé, a different language.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction among sources. Reiter 2011 restates Drude's stem-final rule (stress on the only or last syllable of the lexical root, prefixes unstressed, most suffixes unstressed) and the same exception class (verb stems in final /e/ take penultimate stress, matching Drude 2011 sec. 4 example set (17)). Reiter adds the hedged observation that roots of three or more syllables 'seem to be mostly' penultimate-stressed and says the rules need more research; Drude 2011 treats such cases as listed exceptions to a general stem-final rule, so this is a difference in emphasis, not in placement. Borella 2000, Kamaiurá Sabino 2016 and Corrêa da Silva 2010 make no statement about Awetí stress placement; Corrêa da Silva's final-stress statement concerns Sateré-Mawé.
